nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Blue Mussel
Scientific Name: Mytilus edulis

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Mollusca
Class : Bivalvia
Order: Mytiloida
Family: Mytilidae

Other Common Names:  Common Sea Mussel, edible blue mussel

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Mytilus edulis is not harvested in commercial quantities in the southeastern states due to their lack of abundance. The major commercial harvest on the east coast is from the northeastern states, primarily Maine and Massachusetts (923). From 1955-1977 the U.S. landings averaged approximately 7,000 pounds with a dollar value ranging from 100,000 to a little over 3,000,000 per year (923).

Other:  GET MORE RECENT LANDINGS DATA

nodes.title: Recreational
nodes.body:
Blue mussels are not of major recreational value in the southeast since it occurs only sporadically and in low numbers.

Ecological Role:  Mytilus edulis is not an important ecological link in southeast estuaries due to its low numbers and population instability. In the northeast it can be a major occupier of primary space on hard substrate (rocks, shells, pebbles). Extensive mussel beds also provide a source of food (through biodeposits) and protection for other marine invertebrates (924). Predation pressures occur on all stages of development making blue mussels an important link in connecting phytoplankton production to the benthos and the rest of the estuarine food web. Larval, juvenile, and adult fish feed on the planktonic larvae of Mytilus edulis while birds, starfish, crustaceans, and fish feed on juveniles and adults.

Indicator of environmental stress:
Mytilus edulis is used in the National Status and Trends Program of NOAA (929). The Mussel Watch program within Status and Trends monitors accumulation of pollutants in marine mussels. The blue mussel has also been used in the past to monitor accumulation and loss of radionucleides from nuclear power plant effluents (923).

nodes.title: Overall
nodes.body:
Mytilus edulis is distributed worldwide in subarctic seas (910 924).

Within study area:
The blue mussel is found in North Carolina coastal waters primarily north of Cape Hatteras and occasionally extending into central South Carolina (930 910 924). This species of mussel is found sporadically south of Cape Hatteras due to storms blowing larvae around the Cape. These populations seldom become established with die-offs occurring as temperatures rise in the summer (930). Blue mussels have also been found in deeper, cooler offshore waters (100-499m) allowing its range to extend as far south as Charleston, SC (927).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
The eggs are benthic in low flow environments or are otherwise carried by water currents and turbulence. Trochophore and veliger larval stages are planktonic with plantigrade larvae, juvenile, and adult stages existing as semi-sessile, benthic fauna (924) .

The eggs and early larval stages are subject to movement by water currents. The veliger larvae can migrate vertically through the water column in response to environmental stimuli by use of the ciliary action of the velum (911 9121), and plantigrade larvae are capable of crawling on primary settlement substrates. Once settled, juveniles and adults are semi-sessile. Limited movement is achieved by secreting new byssus threads and adjusting the lengths of existing ones (924).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body: All life stages are found in subtidal marine and estuarine waters (mesohaline-euhaline). Juvenile and adult stages are also intertidal in marine and estuarine waters (924).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body: Maturing larvae (usually < 1.5 mm) initially settle on filamentous substrates such as algae and bryozoans away from the adult population. They then pass through a migratory phase being transported by water currents. During this time they attach and detach from filamentous substrates. At 900 um to 1.5 mm in size they secondarily settle within adult mussel beds (913). Adult and juvenile mussels are usually associated with hard substrate such as rocks (ranging from boulders to pebbles), seawalls, pilings, and jetties. Mud and sand substrates can also be colonized provided there is a solid surface, such as shells or pebbles, for attachment of byssal threads (924).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body: Egg cleavage and early larval development occur normally from 8-18 C with an increasing rate of development as the temperature increases. Egg cleavage does not occur at 5 C and at 20-22 C cleavage is abnormal (914). Larvae held at 5 C for 2 months grow slowly. When subjected to 17 C water they metamorphose but subsequent growth is slower than for larvae that have not been subjected to extended periods of cold (5 C) (914). Larvae have survived experimental temperatures ranging from 5 to greater than 20 C with optimum growth occurring at 20 C and 25-35 ppt (920). Permanent populations of blue mussels do not develop where summer water temperatures exceed 27 C (930 923). Similarly, the laboratory determined upper lethal temperature for Mytilus edulis is 27-29 C (916). Low temperatures, even freezing, may be tolerated for extended periods of time. Recovery after decreased water temperatures is impossible if the tissue temperature drops below 10 to -15 C (931). Water temperatures this low, however, are not experienced by field populations of mussels.

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body: The optimum salinity for larval growth may depend on whether the adult population is oceanic or estuarine. Larvae from oceanic populations develop in salinities ranging from approximately 24-40 ppt with optimum growth occurring between 30-32 ppt (euhaline). Estuarine larvae may develop in salinities as low as 14 ppt (mesohaline) with optimum growth occurring between 20-30 ppt at 16 C and between 17.5-26 ppt at 13 C (914 920). Larvae survive at < 20 ppt and at approximately 40 ppt but growth is often decreased (920). The range of salinities allowing normal larval development is narrower than the range tolerated by adults. Juvenile and adult mussels are euryhaline occurring in salinities ranging from sea water (34 ppt) to mesohaline (5-18 ppt) estuarine waters (924).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Reproduction is primarily sexual with separate male and female sexes (dioecious) (926 924). Rare instances of hermaphroditism have been known to occur (926).

Reproductive Periodicity:  Spawning occurs in the late spring through the summer (generally April-September) in the northeastern United States (925). Southeast populations most likely die off before reaching the age and size of sexual maturity (930).

Fertilization: Eggs and sperm are broadcasted into the water column resulting in external fertilization. Eggs hatch within 4-5 hours at 18 C (921 924).

Fecundity:  Based on mantle weight loss estimates of gamete production are 1 X 107 eggs per gram of tissue weight and 1.1 X 1011 sperm per gram of tissue weight (928).

nodes.title: GROWTH
nodes.body:
Egg:  Egg development is oviparous. The egg progresses through cleavage with the first polar body appearing 18-20 minutes after fertilization. Within 5-20 hours it develops to the free swimming trochophore larval stage.
Larvae:  The larval period lasts between 15 and 35 days depending on the environmental conditions (915 924). There are three major larval stages; the ciliated trocophore (70-110 pm), the veliger (110-260 pm) (which includes the prodissoconch I and II, the eyed larval, and the pediveliger larval stages), and the plantigrade (0.26-1.5 mrn).
Juvenile:  The plantigrade larvae settles on filamentous materials and crawls about or attaches itself loosely. At 900 pm to 1.5 mm the larvae reenters the plankton, seeks a permanent settling site, and begins to metamorphose into a juvenile (913).
Adult:  Sexual maturity is usually reached by the end of the first year but may take as long as 3
years depending on environmental conditions (924). The maximum age and size attained by mussels is approximately 4-5 years and 5.5 cm for populations at lower latitudes while more northerly populations may reach an age of 11-12 years and a size of 9.5 cm (924) .

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: The trochophore larval stage is non-feeding. The veliger larvae, juveniles, and adults are all suspension feeders (924). The veligers filter nanoplankton (924) and the juveniles and adults filter diatoms, protozoa, detritus, and other plankton (921). Phytoplankton cells are the primary food source for all life stages. Silt, when present in low concentrations (922 917), and bacteria present on detritus may also add nutrition to their diet (919).
